facts.statement: Amargasaurus was described by Salgado and Bonaparte in 1991.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Salgado & Bonaparte, 1991

facts.statement: Amargasaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the Aptian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous (Barremian to Aptian),

facts.statement: The only known skeleton of Amargasaurus was discovered in 1984 and is virtually complete, though it includes only a fragmentary skull.
facts.quote: The only known skeleton was discovered in 1984 and is virtually complete, including a fragmentary skull

facts.statement: Amargasaurus was discovered in sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus was discovered in sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation

facts.statement: The La Amarga Formation, where Amargasaurus was found, dates back to the Barremian and Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus was discovered in sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation, which dates back to the Barremian and Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous

facts.statement: Amargasaurus probably fed at mid-height, based on the orientation of its inner ear and neck vertebrae articulation.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus probably fed at mid-height, as shown by the orientation of its inner ear and the articulation of its neck vertebrae

facts.statement: Amargasaurus is classified as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae within the order Sauropoda.
facts.quote: Within the Sauropoda, Amargasaurus is classified as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: Amargasaurus is distinctively characterized by two parallel rows of tall spines running down its neck and back, which are taller than those of any other known sauropod.
facts.quote: Most distinctively, it sported two parallel rows of tall spines down its neck and back, taller than in any other known sauropod

facts.statement: Amargasaurus was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 13 meters in length and weighing approximately 2.5 to 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 13 m in length and weighing approximately 2.5 - 4 MT

facts.statement: Amargasaurus had a shorter neck than most other sauropods, a trait common within the family Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: The neck of Amargasaurus was shorter than in most other sauropods, a common trait within the Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: The neck of Amargasaurus consisted of thirteen opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae that formed ball-and-socket joints with neighboring vertebrae.
facts.quote: The neck consisted of thirteen cervical vertebrae, which were opisthocoelous (convex at the front and hollow at the back), forming ball-and-socket joints with neighboring vertebrae

facts.statement: The tallest spines of Amargasaurus were located on the middle part of the neck, reaching 60 cm in length on the 8th cervical vertebra.
facts.quote: The tallest spines could be found on the middle part of the neck, where they reached 60 cm on the 8th cervical

facts.statement: Only the rear part of the Amargasaurus skull is preserved.
facts.quote: Only the rear part of the skull is preserved

facts.statement: The only known skeleton of Amargasaurus (specimen MACN-N 15) was discovered in February 1984 by Guillermo Rougier during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
facts.quote: The only known skeleton (specimen number MACN-N 15) was discovered in February 1984 by Guillermo Rougier during an expedition led by Argentine paleontologist José Bonaparte

facts.statement: The discovery site of Amargasaurus is located in the La Amarga arroyo in the Picún Leufú Department of Neuquén Province, 70 km south of Zapala.
facts.quote: The discovery site is located in the La Amarga arroyo in the Picún Leufú Department of Neuquén Province in northern Patagonia, 70 km south of Zapala

facts.statement: The official description of Amargasaurus was published in 1991 by Leonardo Salgado and Bonaparte in the Argentinian journal Ameghiniana.
facts.quote: The official description, written in Spanish, was published in 1991 by Leonardo Salgado and Bonaparte in the Argentinian scientific journal Ameghiniana

facts.statement: The species Amargasaurus cazaui is named in honor of Luis Cazau, a geologist with the YPF oil company.
facts.quote: The one species (A. cazaui) is named in honor of Luis Cazau, a geologist with the YPF oil company

facts.statement: Luis Cazau informed Bonaparte's team about the significance of the La Amarga Formation in 1983, which led to the discovery of the skeleton.
facts.quote: In 1983, Cazau informed Bonaparte's team about the paleontological significance of the La Amarga Formation, leading to the discovery of the skeleton

facts.statement: Amargasaurus is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae, which is a clade inside the superfamily Diplodocoidea.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus is classified as a member of the Dicraeosauridae, a family ranked clade within the Diplodocoidea.

facts.statement: Amargasaurus was the first known dicraeosaurid dinosaur from the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus was the first dicraeosaurid known from the Cretaceous

facts.statement: Members of the Diplodocoidea, including Amargasaurus, had box-shaped snouts and narrow teeth restricted to the front of their jaws.
facts.quote: All members of the Diplodocoidea are characterized by their box-shaped snout and narrow teeth restricted to the foremost portion of the jaws.

facts.statement: Amargasaurus exhibits the most extreme elongation of bifurcated neural spines among dicraeosaurids.
facts.quote: In the Dicraeosauridae, the bifurcated neural spines were strongly elongated, a trend reaching its extreme in Amargasaurus.

facts.statement: The exact function and life appearance of Amargasaurus's elongated vertebral spines remain unknown.
facts.quote: Both the function and the appearance in life of the extremely elongated and bifurcated vertebral spines remain elusive.

facts.statement: Salgado and Bonaparte (1991) hypothesized that the spines served as defensive weapons because they tapered toward their tips.
facts.quote: Salgado and Bonaparte, in 1991, suggested the spines represented defense weapons against predators, arguing that they tapered towards their tips.

facts.statement: Some researchers have proposed that the spines supported two parallel skin sails for display.
facts.quote: Some subsequently published life restorations showed the double row of spines supporting two parallel skin sails.

facts.statement: Jack Bailey (1997) suggested the spines resembled those of sail-bearing pelycosaurs and that Amargasaurus might have possessed a single skin sail.
facts.quote: Jack Bailey, in 1997, argued that the spines resembled those of sail-bearing pelycosaurs like Dimetrodon.

facts.statement: Jack Bailey suggested that dinosaurs with elongated spines like Spinosaurus and Ouranosaurus may have had fleshy humps above their hips.
facts.quote: Bailey suggested similar humps for other dinosaurs with strongly elongated neural spines, such as Spinosaurus and Ouranosaurus.

facts.statement: Striations on the spines suggest they were covered by either keratin or skin, similar to modern bovid horn cores.
facts.quote: A cover of either keratin or skin is indicated striations on the surface of the spines similar to those of bony horn cores of today's bovids.

facts.statement: Hallett and Wedel (2016) hypothesized that Amargasaurus could have used its backwards-directed spines to skewer predators during a neck-snapping attack.
facts.quote: In 2016, Mark Hallett and Mathew Wedel suggested that the backwards-directed spines might have been able to skewer predators when the neck was abruptly drawn backwards during an attack.

facts.statement: In 2014, researchers CT-scanned the skull of Amargasaurus to create three-dimensional models of its brain cavity and inner ear.
facts.quote: Paulina Carabajal and colleagues, in 2014, CT-scanned the skull, allowing for the generation of three-dimensional models of both the cranial endocast (the cast of the brain cavity) and the inner ear.

facts.statement: The volume of the cranial endocast of Amargasaurus was measured between 94 and 98 milliliters.
facts.quote: The cranial endocast was shown to encompass 94 to 98 ml in volume.

facts.statement: The inner ear of Amargasaurus measured 30 millimeters in height and 22 millimeters in width.
facts.quote: The inner ear was 30 mm tall and 22 mm wide.

facts.statement: Research suggests Amargasaurus had poorer hearing than other studied sauropods because its inner ear lagena was relatively short.
facts.quote: The lagena, the part containing the hair cells for hearing, was rather short, indicating that the sense of hearing would have been poorer in Amargasaurus than in other sauropods for which inner ears have been studied.

facts.statement: Based on inner ear models, researchers suggested Amargasaurus held its snout at a downward angle of approximately 65 degrees relative to the horizontal.
facts.quote: Using their three-dimensional model of the inner ear, Carabajal and colleagues suggested that the snout faced downwards at an angle of roughly 65° relative to the horizontal.

facts.statement: In a neutral posture, the snout of Amargasaurus would have rested about 80 centimeters above the ground.
facts.quote: According to Carabajal and colleagues, the neck was gently sloping downwards, so that the snout would have rested 80 cm above the ground in neutral posture.

facts.statement: The elongated neural spines of Amargasaurus likely prevented its neck from being raised higher than 270 centimeters.
facts.quote: Raising of the neck, e.g. for reaching an alert position, would have been constricted by the elongated neural spines, not permitting heights greater than 270 cm.

facts.statement: Anatomical features suggest Amargasaurus had increased head mobility, allowing it to graze or uproot vegetation while feeding low to the ground.
facts.quote: These features indicate an increased head mobility and an ability to graze or uproot vegetation, which would have been helpful when feeding low above the ground.

facts.statement: In 1991, Salgado and Bonaparte proposed that Amargasaurus was a slow walker due to its proportionally short forearms and lower legs.
facts.quote: Salgado and Bonaparte, in 1991, suggested that Amargasaurus was a slow walker, as both the forearms and lower legs were proportionally short, as a feature common to slow-moving animals.

facts.statement: In 1999, Mazzetta and Fariña contradicted the slow-walker hypothesis, arguing that Amargasaurus was capable of rapid locomotion.
facts.quote: This was contradicted by Gerardo Mazzetta and Richard Fariña in 1999, who argued that Amargasaurus was capable of rapid locomotion.

facts.statement: The leg bones of Amargasaurus were sturdier than those of the modern white rhinoceros, an animal adapted for galloping.
facts.quote: The leg bones of Amargasaurus were even more sturdy than those of today's white rhinoceros, which is adapted to galloping.

facts.statement: Analysis of growth lines in a rib indicates that the holotype individual of Amargasaurus was at least ten years old.
facts.quote: The rib showed the most complete record of lines of arrested growth, indicating that the Amargasaurus holotype individual was at least ten years old.

facts.statement: The absence of an external fundamental system in the bone suggests the individual may not have been fully grown, though erosion could also explain this missing layer.
facts.quote: However, an external fundamental system (a layer containing very closely spaced lines of arrested growth) is missing, possibly indicating that the individual was not yet fully grown, although it cannot be excluded that the external fundamental system was originally present but has since been eroded.

facts.statement: Amargasaurus fossils come from the La Amarga Formation in the Neuquén Basin, dating to the Barremian and late Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus stems from sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation, which is part of the Neuquén Basin and dates to the Barremian and late Aptian of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Evidence from its neck and inner ear anatomy suggests Amargasaurus fed at heights of up to 2.7 meters above the ground.
facts.quote: Amargasaurus probably fed above ground level at heights of up to 2.7 m, as evidenced by the anatomy of its neck and inner ear.

facts.statement: The genus Amargasaurus was named by Bonaparte in 1984.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Amargasaurus (genus), Bonaparte 1984

facts.quote: Family: Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: Amargasaurus is a member of the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: Amargasaurus lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Barremian (125.77 to 121.4 million years ago)
